title: Data Center Is Fined $1.1 Million for Operating 62 Power Generators

reading.body:
This is a compliance failure at the power layer of a data center build, not a failure of any model or software. State inspectors found 62 natural gas generators, each rated at 2,000 kilowatts, installed and running at the Vineland site without permits to be installed or operated. The fine of $1.07 million was issued for violating New Jersey's Air Pollution Control Act, and officials described it as the largest ever given to a New Jersey data center operator.

The failure sits in the provisioning stage of the deployment, before the campus is finished. The site is slated for completion at the end of the year and some of it is already in use, so equipment was brought online ahead of the approvals that would have made its operation lawful. Catching this would have required a permit check before the generators were installed and before they were run, and the surrounding complaints, a federal lawsuit from homeowners over persistent noise and violation orders from the Cumberland County Health Department, indicate the site's effects were already drawing official attention.

What the reporting does not establish is intent. The fine is a finding on permit violations, the federal lawsuit is an allegation rather than a verdict, and the reports do not state whether the compute at this site is used for AI.

reports.title: Data Center Is Fined $1.1 Million for Operating 62 Power Generators

summary:
New Jersey fined DataOne $1.07 million after state inspectors found 62 generators the size of tractor trailers at its Vineland data center site in late July. The generators run on natural gas, each with 2,000 kilowatts of capacity, and none had permits to be installed or operated. The fine, issued Tuesday, was for violating the state's Air Pollution Control Act and is the largest ever given to a New Jersey data center operator, officials said.

The Vineland campus is slated for completion at the end of the year. It will be a 2.6 million square foot complex needing 350 megawatts, enough to power a medium size city. Some of it is already in use. The site has drawn complaints, including a federal lawsuit from homeowners over persistent noise and violation orders from the Cumberland County Health Department for excessive noise. Governor Mikie Sherrill said at a Climate Week event that building such projects must benefit New Jersey communities.
